title: Krylov complexity and the growth of the black hole interior in 3D gravity
authors: Arpan Bhattacharyya, Sounak Pal, Juan F. Pedraza
abstract: We investigate the growth of the black hole interior in three-dimensional gravity from the boundary theory. For the two-sided BTZ black hole, we propose a boundary reconstruction of the time dependence of a codimension-one surface in terms of correlation functions of smeared operators in the thermofield double state, reproducing the characteristic late-time linear growth predicted by the complexity-volume proposal. Using the Chern--Simons formulation of three-dimensional gravity, these nonlocal correlators are represented by bulk Wilson lines with smeared endpoints, extending the familiar connection between Wilson lines and codimension-two observables underlying holographic entanglement entropy to codimension-one observables. We then ask whether the same geometric growth is captured by Krylov complexity. For the smeared operators, we extract the Lanczos data from their correlation functions and find that operator Krylov complexity reproduces the late-time linear growth of the black hole interior, extending previous connections between operator growth and bulk geometry to AdS$_3$. By contrast, the Krylov spread complexity of the thermofield double state, obtained from the semiclassical gravitational partition function, does not exhibit the linear growth of the bulk volume within the regime accessible to our analysis. Our results therefore point to a distinguished role for operator Krylov complexity in encoding black hole interior growth beyond two-dimensional gravity, while highlighting a qualitative distinction between operator and state notions of Krylov complexity.
summary: This theoretical paper studies black hole interior growth in 3D gravity using the AdS/CFT correspondence. By comparing two complexity measures, the authors find that operator Krylov complexity correctly captures the expected linear growth of the black hole interior volume. This result establishes a novel diagnostic tool, suggesting that operator complexity is the appropriate measure for encoding bulk geometric growth in this holographic setting.
main_problem: The paper investigates the growth of the black hole interior in three-dimensional gravity and determines whether this geometric growth is captured by the operator Krylov complexity measure.
main_result: Operator Krylov complexity successfully reproduces the characteristic late-time linear growth of the black hole interior, while the state-based Krylov spread complexity does not, highlighting a distinction between the two complexity notions.
method: The authors use the AdS/CFT correspondence, employing the Chern-Simons formulation of 3D gravity to relate boundary correlation functions of smeared operators to bulk Wilson lines, and then apply Krylov methods to analyze the resulting dynamics.
model_or_system: The physical system is the two-sided BTZ black hole in three-dimensional gravity, analyzed via its dual description using the Thermofield Double (TFD) state in AdS$_3$. The analysis compares two complexity measures: operator Krylov complexity and Krylov spread complexity.
key_observables: Operator Krylov complexity, Krylov spread complexity, codimension-one surface volume, and the effective representation parameter $\kappa_{	ext{eff}}(t)$.
important_parameters: The late-time linear growth regime of the black hole interior volume, and the semiclassical approximation regime for the partition function.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the semiclassical approximation and focuses on the linear growth regime, not the eventual non-perturbative saturation of the interior volume.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically compares probing a codimension-two object via a Wilson line versus extending this to probe a codimension-one surface using smeared operators. Figure 2 illustrates the integration regions for the Euclidean time coordinate associated with the codimension-one area.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the boundary reconstruction of the black hole interior growth using correlation functions. It then calculates and compares the growth rates derived from operator Krylov complexity versus Krylov spread complexity, concluding with a discussion on the implications for complexity measures in AdS$_3$.
why_interesting: The work extends the use of complexity measures beyond standard quantum information diagnostics, applying them to fundamental gravitational physics (black hole interiors) and providing a concrete, testable distinction between operator and state complexity in this context.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic representation of the boundary and bulk constructions. On the left, a Wilson line connecting boundary insertions probes a codimension-two bulk object in AdS3. On the right, we extend this construction by smearing the boundary operators along the periodically identified spatial direction ϕ. The resulting non-local operators provide the boundary observable used to probe the growth of the codimension-one surface extending through the black hole interior.

Figure 2: Integration regions for the Euclidean time coordinate τ associated with the extended codimension-one area in AdS3. The left panel corresponds to the two-sided correlator, while the right panel shows the corresponding single-boundary correlator.
Figure 3: Late-time growth of the codimension-one observable AL|R(C), showing the asymptotically linear regime.

Figure 4: Schematic illustration of operator spreading for an initially local operator (left) and an extended non-local operator (right). A local operator is initially spatially localized, whereas the extended operator already has nontrivial spatial support at t = 0. This distinction concerns the spatial structure of the seed operator in configuration space; in the Krylov representation, either operator defines a single initial basis element O0, and their subsequent dynamics is encoded in the corresponding Lanczos data.
Figure 5: Dependence of the Lanczos coefficients an and bn on the inverse temperature β. The left column corresponds to c = 10, and the right column to c = 30.
